items.titleEnglish: What is the future of work?
items.contentMarkdown:
Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "What is the future of work?"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2024/ep-240201

Activity type: listening for predictions and opinions about the future of work.
Language focus: predictions with will and won't, and plans (plan to continue, going to).

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Which two predictions from the 1930s does Beth mention? (gist)
2) What did Elon Musk predict about artificial intelligence? (detail)
3) Which prediction about work came true during Covid? (detail)
4) What does "take something with a pinch of salt" mean? (vocabulary)
5) What is Andrew Palmer's worry about AI and jobs? (detail)
6) How many of the sixty companies planned to continue with the four-day week? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: Smell-o-vision — a television that lets you smell things — and a miracle pill that cures all diseases. They have not come true.
- Q2: That AI will eventually mean that no one will have to work.
- Q3: Millions of people were forced to work from home.
- Q4: Not to believe it completely, because it may not be true.
- Q5: A sequencing risk: AI will replace some jobs and new jobs will crop up, but not at the same time — there won't be coordination.
- Q6: 92% (answer c), because it was popular with bosses and workers.

Phrase-capture instruction: write down every sentence with will or won't that you hear, for example "there won't be coordination". Then write two predictions about your own project with will and two plans with going to.

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Life in the modern office"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2022/ep-220505

Activity type: listening for details about workplaces and how people organise their space.
Language focus: the present continuous for changes that are happening now (more and more people are returning to the office) and workplace vocabulary.

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Why is Neil annoyed at the start of the programme? (gist)
2) What is hot-desking? (vocabulary)
3) What is an open-plan office, and why do companies use it? (detail)
4) Name two objects that workers use to mark out their own space. (detail)
5) What did the young woman do with her photo montage every day? (detail)
6) What was British workers' number one complaint about office life? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: Someone has taken his pen and his coffee mug since the office started hot-desking.
- Q2: A system where workers do not have their own desk; they use any free desk each day.
- Q3: A large space without internal walls. The idea is to create a sense of togetherness.
- Q4: Any two: family photos, holiday souvenirs, home-made cakes or biscuits, plants, postcards.
- Q5: She rolled it up and pinned it to the divider of whatever desk she was using, to feel a sense of familiarity.
- Q6: People speaking too loudly (answer b).

Phrase-capture instruction: listen for the present continuous (more and more people are returning to work in the office). Then write two sentences about changes that are happening in your workplace or university now, and one arrangement for next week.

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Why do we procrastinate?"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2023/ep-230216

Activity type: listening for reasons and advice about deadlines and delays.
Language focus: time expressions and future time clauses (until the last minute, when a deadline is approaching, before you end up ...).

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Why does Sam want to start the programme quickly? (gist)
2) What is a procrastinator? (vocabulary)
3) Which problems are linked with procrastination? (detail)
4) Why does the comedian Eshaan Akbar say that he procrastinates? (detail)
5) According to the theory of evolution in the programme, why do we procrastinate? (detail)
6) What two tips does Neil give, and what percentage of people have a serious procrastination problem? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: She has a deadline today and she hasn't finished her work.
- Q2: Someone who keeps delaying things that need to be done.
- Q3: Higher stress, lower wellbeing, and lower financial and career success.
- Q4: He tells himself that he works better under pressure.
- Q5: Our ancestors were impulsive. In modern life, when we are impulsive and get distracted, we put things off. It is an emotional response, not only a time-management problem.
- Q6: Break the task into smaller stages, and forgive yourself for procrastinating in the past. About 20% of people (answer b).

Phrase-capture instruction: note the time phrases you hear (until the last minute, when a deadline is approaching). Then write a plan for one project task with when, before and as soon as, for example: "As soon as the parts arrive, I'll start the assembly."

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Building rapport with others"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-210617

Activity type: listening for ideas about communication styles at work.
Language focus: polite, friendly communication at work (being frank but not sarcastic) and the phrasal verb get on with.

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) What do Neil and Georgina know about each other after working together for a long time? (gist)
2) What does "get on with someone" mean? (vocabulary)
3) Who is Emily Alison, and who does she work with? (detail)
4) Why does Emily compare building rapport to walking a tightrope? (meaning)
5) Emily names four communication styles after animals. Which animal is the best at building rapport? (detail)
6) What is the title of Dale Carnegie's famous book? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: Georgina knows that Neil eats egg and tomato sandwiches; Neil knows that Georgina hates it when people don't wash their cups in the staff kitchen.
- Q2: To like someone and have a friendly relationship with them.
- Q3: A psychologist who works with the police to build rapport with criminal suspects. She wrote a book about rapport.
- Q4: You must keep a careful balance: be objective and show compassion without being sympathetic or collusive.
- Q5: The friendly, cooperative monkey. The others are the bossy lion, the passive mouse and the T-Rex (conflict).
- Q6: How to Win Friends and Influence People (answer c).

Phrase-capture instruction: write down the words for good and bad communication (get on with, frank, sarcastic). Then write three polite requests or suggestions to a colleague with Could you, Would you mind and Shall we.

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Flexible working"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-210715

Activity type: listening for facts and opinions about flexible working.
Language focus: comparatives and superlatives (more flexible, the longest hours, the fewest hours, more likely).

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) How does Georgina describe office work today? (gist)
2) What is Georgina's quiz question? (detail)
3) According to Sarah Jackson, what does flexible working really mean? (detail)
4) In the UK, who has had the right to request flexible working since 2014? (detail)
5) What bias does Sarah Jackson describe? (detail)
6) Which country works the longest hours, and which works the fewest? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: It doesn't have to be a fixed routine; it is much more flexible these days.
- Q2: Workers from which country work the longest hours, according to the OECD: South Korea, Germany or Mexico?
- Q3: It is not only working from home. It means choice and control over when, where and how long you work, agreed with your manager.
- Q4: Everyone, including men. At first the law was only for parents of young or disabled children.
- Q5: Men are more likely to have their requests for flexible working turned down.
- Q6: Mexico — about 2,255 hours a year, around 43 hours a week (answer c). Germans work the fewest hours.

Phrase-capture instruction: write down the comparatives and superlatives you hear (more flexible, the longest, the fewest, more likely). Then compare two ways of working, for example office work and remote work, in three sentences.

Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "No more bosses"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english/ep-200806

Activity type: listening for how a company works without managers.
Language focus: quantity words and teamwork language (some, others, many, more; commitment, accountable).

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) According to Neil, why do some workers have problems with their bosses? (gist)
2) What is a hierarchy? (vocabulary)
3) Which company was one of the first to try self-management, and what are its two principles? (detail)
4) How are decisions made at Morning Star? (detail)
5) What is one possible problem with having no bosses? (detail)
6) How much do extra management and bureaucracy cost the US economy every year? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: They feel that managers don't listen to them, or because most companies are hierarchies.
- Q2: A system that organises people by their level of importance — managers on top, workers below.
- Q3: Morning Star, a tomato grower in California. People should not use force or coercion against others, and people should keep the commitments they make.
- Q4: By all employees equally, without coercion. Work is based on requests and responses.
- Q5: The extra responsibility can create more work and stress, and some people may get left behind.
- Q6: About 3 trillion dollars (answer c).

Phrase-capture instruction: listen for quantity words (some people, others, more managers, a lot of money). Then write three sentences about the resources and people in your project with many, a few, enough and too many.

items.contentMarkdown:
Source: BBC Learning English — 6 Minute English: "Is it OK to disagree?"
URL: https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2026/ep-260101

Activity type: listening for advice about calm discussion and disagreement.
Language focus: calm, polite disagreement and the pattern the more ..., the more ...

Listening focus (choose one):
- Steady (about 1 minute): listen to the opening, up to the quiz question. Answer questions 1–2.
- Balanced (about 2–3 minutes): listen to the first half of the episode. Answer questions 1–4.
- Intensive (about 4–6 minutes): listen to the whole episode twice — first for the main ideas, then for details. Answer questions 1–6.

Comprehension questions (steady: 1–2; balanced: 1–4; intensive: 1–6):
1) Does Neil usually have the same opinions as his friends, or different ones? (gist)
2) How can social media algorithms affect our opinions? (detail)
3) What does Professor Paul Dolan suggest people do before they send a message on social media? (detail)
4) How long does it take the amygdala to calm down when we are very angry? (detail)
5) What did the dating experiment find about open-mindedness? (detail)
6) What is the silver bullet for a less divided society, and what percentage of British people think society is divided? (quiz answer)

Answer key (check after you save):
- Q1: Quite similar opinions — that is partly why they are friends.
- Q2: They tend to show us what we already like and agree with.
- Q3: Wait five minutes — take time to calm down, for example with a deep breath.
- Q4: About 15 minutes, but it starts to calm down within a few seconds.
- Q5: People want an open-minded, tolerant partner, but they don't want to be very open-minded themselves.
- Q6: Get offline and meet people who are different from you. 80% (answer c).

Phrase-capture instruction: write down the sentence "the more you're around people that are different, the more you realise ...". Then write two polite sentences that disagree with a colleague's idea and suggest a compromise, for example: "I see your point, but what if we ...?"
